title: I. Kolya Krassotkin
paragraphs: It was early November. A hard frost had set in, eleven degrees Réaumur, but there was no snow. A little dry snow had fallen on the frozen ground during the night, though, and a sharp, dry wind was picking it up and driving it along the dreary streets of our town, especially around the market-place. The morning was dull, but the snow had stopped.

Not far from the market-place, close to Plotnikov’s shop, there was a small house, very clean inside and out. It belonged to Madame Krassotkin, widow of a former provincial secretary, who had died fourteen years earlier. She was still a nice-looking woman of thirty-two, and she lived in her neat little house on her private means. Her life was one of respectable seclusion, and her nature was soft but fairly cheerful. She had been about eighteen when her husband died. They had been married only a year, and she had just borne him a son. Since the day he died she had given herself heart and soul to raising her precious treasure, her boy Kolya. For those fourteen years she had loved him passionately, yet he had brought her far more pain than happiness. Nearly every day she shook and almost fainted with fear that he would fall ill, catch cold, do something naughty, or climb on a chair and fall off it, and so on and so on. Once Kolya started school, his mother took up all the sciences herself so as to study them with him and help him with his lessons. She made a point of getting to know the teachers and their wives. She even made up to Kolya’s schoolfellows and fawned on them, hoping that this would keep Kolya from being teased, laughed at or beaten. She carried it so far that the boys began to mock him because of her, taunting him as a “mother’s darling.”

But the boy could stand up for himself. He was a resolute boy, “tremendously strong,” as the rumor went in his class, and he soon showed that it was true. He was agile, strong-willed, bold and enterprising. He did well at lessons, and word went around the school that he could beat the teacher, Dardanelov, at arithmetic and universal history. He looked down on everybody, yet he was a good comrade and never lofty about it. He took his schoolfellows’ respect as only his due, but he stayed friendly with them. Above all, he knew where to draw the line. When he had to, he could hold himself back, and with the teachers he never crossed that last mystic boundary beyond which a prank turns into an unpardonable breach of discipline. Still, on every possible occasion he loved mischief as much as the smallest boy in the school. It was less the mischief itself he wanted than the sensation: to think up something effective, something that people would notice. He was extremely vain. He even knew how to make his mother give way to him, and he ruled her almost like a despot. She gave way—oh, she had been giving way for years. The one thought she could not endure was that her boy did not love her much. She was forever fancying that Kolya was “unfeeling” toward her. At times she would dissolve in hysterical tears and reproach him with his coldness. The boy disliked this, and the more he was asked to show feeling, the more he seemed to dodge it on purpose. But it was not on purpose; it was instinct. It was simply his character. His mother was wrong: he was very fond of her. He just disliked “sheepish sentimentality,” as he called it in his schoolboy language.

The house had a bookcase holding a few books that had been his father’s. Kolya liked reading, and he had read several of them on his own. His mother did not mind. Sometimes she merely wondered at the sight of the boy standing for hours at the bookcase, absorbed in a book, instead of running off to play. That was how Kolya came to read some things not suitable for his age.

As a rule the boy knew where to draw the line in his mischief. Lately, though, he had begun to play pranks that gave his mother real alarm. There was nothing vicious in them, it is true, but they showed a wild, mad recklessness.

That July, during the summer holidays, mother and son traveled to another district, forty-five miles away, to spend a week with a distant relation. The relation’s husband was an official at the railway station (the very station, nearest to our town, from which a month later Ivan Fyodorovitch Karamazov left for Moscow). Kolya began by studying every detail of the railways with great care, since he knew he could impress his schoolfellows with his new knowledge when he got home. But other boys happened to be about, and he soon made friends with them. Some lived at the station and others in the neighborhood. There were six or seven of them, all between twelve and fifteen, and two came from our town. The boys played together, and on the fourth or fifth day of Kolya’s stay, the foolish lads made a mad bet. Kolya was nearly the youngest of them, and the others rather looked down on him for it. Out of vanity, or reckless bravado, he bet them two roubles that he would lie down between the rails at night, when the eleven o’clock train was due, and stay there without moving while it rolled over him at full speed. They did look into it first, it is true, and found that a person could lie so flat between the rails that a train would pass right over without touching him. But actually lying there was no joke! Kolya stoutly insisted that he would do it. They laughed at him at first and called him a little liar and a braggart, but that only egged him on. What stung him most was that these fifteen-year-olds turned up their noses at him so haughtily. At first they had been inclined to treat him as “a small boy,” unfit to keep their company, and that was an insult he could not bear.

So they decided to go that evening, half a mile from the station, so that the train would have time to reach full speed after leaving it. The boys gathered. The night was pitch-dark, without a moon. At the agreed time Kolya lay down between the rails. The other five, who had taken the bet, waited in the bushes below the embankment. Their hearts pounded with suspense, which gave way to alarm and remorse. At last they heard the train rumbling in the distance as it left the station. Two red lights gleamed out of the darkness, and the monster roared as it came on.

“Run, run away from the rails,” the boys cried to Kolya from the bushes, breathless with terror. But it was too late. The train rushed up and flew past. The boys ran to Kolya. He lay there without moving. They started tugging at him and lifting him up. Suddenly he got to his feet and walked off without a word. Later he explained that he had lain there as if unconscious in order to scare them. The truth, as he admitted to his mother long afterward, was that he had really lost consciousness. So his reputation as “a desperate character” was fixed forever. He went back to the station as white as a sheet. The next day he had a slight attack of nervous fever, but he was in high spirits and very pleased with himself. The incident did not come out at once. When they returned to town, however, it reached the school and even the ears of the masters. Then Kolya’s mother hurried to beg the masters to be lenient with her boy, and in the end Dardanelov, a respected and influential teacher, put in a word for him, and the matter was let drop.

Dardanelov was a middle-aged bachelor who had been passionately in love with Madame Krassotkin for many years. Some time before, about a year earlier, he had once ventured, trembling with fear and delicacy of feeling, to offer her his hand most respectfully. She had flatly refused him, feeling that accepting would betray her son. Yet certain mysterious signs gave Dardanelov reason to believe that the charming but all too chaste and tender-hearted widow did not find him repulsive. Kolya’s mad prank seemed to have broken the ice. Dardanelov was rewarded for pleading for the boy with a hint of hope. The hint was a faint one, it is true, but Dardanelov was such a paragon of purity and delicacy that for the time being it was enough to make him perfectly happy. He was fond of the boy, though he thought it beneath him to try to win him over, and in class he was severe and strict with him. Kolya, for his part, kept him at a respectful distance. He knew his lessons perfectly, ranked second in his class, and was reserved with Dardanelov. The whole class firmly believed that Kolya was so good at universal history that he could “beat” even Dardanelov. Indeed, Kolya had once asked him, “Who founded Troy?” Dardanelov gave a very vague reply, speaking of the movements and migrations of peoples, of how remote the period was, of the mythical legends. But who had founded Troy, meaning which individuals, he could not say, and for some reason he even considered the question idle and frivolous. The boys, however, stayed convinced that Dardanelov did not know who founded Troy. Kolya had read about the founders of Troy in Smaragdov, whose history was among the books in his father’s bookcase. In the end all the boys grew curious about who had founded Troy, but Krassotkin would not give up his secret, and his reputation for learning stood unshaken.

After the railway incident, Kolya’s manner toward his mother changed somewhat. When Anna Fyodorovna (Madame Krassotkin) heard of her son’s exploit, she nearly went out of her mind with horror. Her hysterics were so terrible, and went on with only short breaks for several days, that Kolya was seriously alarmed at last and gave his word of honor that such pranks would never happen again. At Madame Krassotkin’s insistence he swore it on his knees before the holy image, and swore it by his father’s memory. The “manly” Kolya burst into tears like a boy of six. All that day mother and son kept rushing into each other’s arms, sobbing. The next day Kolya woke up as “unfeeling” as ever, but he had grown quieter, more modest, sterner and more thoughtful.

Six weeks later he did get into another scrape, it is true, one that even brought his name to the attention of our Justice of the Peace. But it was a scrape of an entirely different kind, amusing and foolish, and as it turned out he was not the leader in it, only caught up in it. More of that later. His mother still fretted and trembled, and the more uneasy she grew, the higher Dardanelov’s hopes rose. It should be noted that Kolya understood and guessed what was in Dardanelov’s heart, and of course he despised him profoundly for his “feelings.” Before, he had been tactless enough to show this contempt in front of his mother, hinting vaguely that he knew what Dardanelov was after. After the railway incident, though, his behavior in this respect changed too. He allowed himself not the slightest allusion to the subject, and in front of his mother he began to speak of Dardanelov with more respect. The sensitive woman noticed it at once and was boundlessly grateful. But if a visitor merely mentioned Dardanelov in Kolya’s presence, she would blush as pink as a rose. At such moments Kolya would either stare out of the window with a scowl, or look over the state of his boots, or shout angrily for “Perezvon.” Perezvon was the big, shaggy, mangy dog he had picked up a month earlier and brought home. For some reason he kept it hidden indoors and showed it to none of his schoolfellows. He bullied the dog dreadfully and taught it all sorts of tricks. The poor creature howled for him whenever he was away at school, and when he came in it whined with delight, raced about as if it had gone crazy, begged, and lay on the ground playing dead, and so on. In fact it performed every trick it had been taught, not because it was ordered to, but from the sheer zeal of its excited, grateful heart.

I forgot, by the way, to mention that Kolya Krassotkin was the boy who had been stabbed with a penknife by the one the reader already knows as Captain Snegiryov’s son. Ilusha had been defending his father when the schoolboys jeered at him and shouted the nickname “wisp of tow.”
